questions.q: 'The girls gave the boys ___ ball back.' their / his / her?
questions.a: 'their' — the ball belongs to the girls (antecedent), not the nearest noun 'boys'. A wrong answer 'his' or reading it as the boys' ball reveals nearest-noun matching — the classic antecedent error.

questions.q: Fix: 'Its raining, so the dog lost it's bone.'
questions.a: 'It's raining' (it is) + 'its bone' (possessive, no apostrophe). A wrong answer keeping both apostrophes shows the student thinks apostrophe = possession — exactly backwards for 'its'.

questions.q: 'Ravi told Mohan he had passed.' Who passed — and why is it a problem?
questions.a: Cannot tell — 'he' could point to either Ravi or Mohan. Rewrite needed: 'Ravi told Mohan, "I have passed"' or 'Ravi congratulated Mohan on passing'. A wrong answer confidently picking one shows the student doesn't yet see ambiguity as an error.

questions.q: But the ______ must match the original in number and gender — 'Ravi lost HIS book', and it must point clearly to ONE noun, not two.
Fill in the blank: A pronoun replaces a noun so we do not repeat ______: he, she, it, they, this, who, mine.
Fill in the blank: Show the repetition ______ first: 'Ravi picked up Ravi's bag and Ravi left.' Clunky.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student picks the pronoun matching the antecedent's number and gender, spots ambiguous pronouns ('Ravi told Mohan he won' — who won?), and uses possessive pronouns (mine, yours, theirs) correctly.
